Shipping PayGuard was the start, not the finish. Fraudsters adapt, libraries age, servers get patched and the person who built the model moves to another team. **Maintenance** is the steady work that keeps a model useful. Machine learning systems are especially prone to this hidden cost, because they depend on data as well as code ([Sculley et al., 2015](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5656-hidden-technical-debt-in-machine-learning-systems)).

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The five things that decay in a production ML system
- How scheduled, triggered and "never" retraining compare, in a simulation you control
- A routine maintenance calendar
- How to handle an incident, from alert to postmortem
:::

{{< include ../_series-nav.md >}}

## What decays, and how fast

| What decays | Example in PayGuard | Warning sign | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data drift** | New country, bigger payments | PSI rising | Retrain on recent data |
| **Concept drift** | Fraudsters switch to small "test" payments | Precision falls, inputs look normal | Retrain, add new features |
| **Dependencies** | Python or scikit-learn version reaches end of life | Security advisories | Scheduled upgrades with tests |
| **Infrastructure** | Base image has known vulnerabilities | Image scan findings | Rebuild and redeploy regularly |
| **Knowledge** | The builder leaves | Nobody can explain a feature | Model cards, runbooks, docs |

: Sources of decay {#tbl-decay}

**Concept drift** is the sneakiest. The inputs look the same, but their meaning changes: a $5 payment used to be harmless and is now a fraudster testing a stolen card. Only fresh labels reveal it.

## Retraining strategies, simulated

PayGuard's quality slowly decays as patterns shift, and on **day 200** fraudsters change tactics (a sudden concept drift). Compare three strategies over a year. Each retraining costs time and compute, so more is not free.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js"
viewof every = Inputs.range([7, 180], {value: 60, step: 1, label: "Scheduled: retrain every N days"})
viewof trigger = Inputs.range([0.84, 0.92], {value: 0.89, step: 0.005, label: "Triggered: retrain when AUC drops below"})
viewof costEach = Inputs.range([10, 500], {value: 120, step: 10, label: "Cost per retraining ($, example)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
simulate = (rule) => {
  const rnd = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(9))(0, 0.003);
  let last = 0, shockSeen = false, out = [], n = 0, pend = -1;
  for (let d = 0; d < 365; d++) {
    const age = d - last;
    let q = 0.93 - 0.00035 * age - 0.0000009 * age * age;
    if (d >= 200 && last < 200) q -= 0.05;          // new fraud tactic, unseen by the model
    q += rnd();
    out.push({d, q});
    if (rule(d, age, q) && pend < 0) pend = d + 3;  // 3 days to retrain and ship
    if (d === pend) { last = d; n++; pend = -1; }
  }
  return {series: out, n};
}
strategies = [
  {name: "Never retrain", r: simulate(() => false), c: ms.rose},
  {name: `Every ${every} days`, r: simulate((d, age) => age >= every), c: ms.indigo},
  {name: `When AUC < ${trigger}`, r: simulate((d, age, q) => q < trigger), c: ms.teal}
]
Plot.plot({
  ...msStyle, height: 360, width: 760, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Day →"}, y: {label: "↑ AUC on live data", domain: [0.6, 0.95], grid: true},
  color: {domain: strategies.map(s => s.name), range: strategies.map(s => s.c), legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([200], {stroke: ms.amber, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.text([200], {x: d => d, y: 0.935, text: () => "new fraud tactic", dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor", fontSize: 11.5}),
    ...strategies.map(s => Plot.line(s.r.series, {x: "d", y: "q", stroke: () => s.name, strokeWidth: 2.2}))
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(strategies.map(s => ({
  Strategy: s.name, "Avg AUC": d3.mean(s.r.series, d => d.q).toFixed(3),
  "Retrains": s.r.n, "Cost ($)": s.r.n * costEach,
  "Days < 0.85": s.r.series.filter(d => d.q < 0.85).length
})), {layout: "auto"})
```

What the simulation shows:

- **Never retraining** looks fine for weeks, then slides and never recovers from the day-200 shock.
- **Scheduled retraining** is simple and predictable, but a long interval reacts slowly to the shock, and a short one wastes money in calm periods.
- **Triggered retraining** reacts to real problems, but it needs trustworthy quality signals. Because fraud labels arrive late (see [Monitoring](/deployment/monitoring/model-monitoring-drift.qmd)), teams usually trigger on **drift signals plus a maximum age**, for example "retrain when PSI > 0.2 or every 60 days, whichever comes first".

## A routine maintenance calendar

Small, regular tasks prevent big emergencies.

```{python}
#| label: fig-calendar
#| fig-cap: "One quarter of PayGuard upkeep. Each bar is a scheduled task."
#| code-fold: true
import pandas as pd, plotly.express as px
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG
tasks = []
for d in pd.date_range("2026-10-05", "2026-12-28", freq="7D"):
    tasks.append(("Review drift and alerts", "Weekly", d, d + pd.Timedelta(days=1)))
for d in ["2026-10-01", "2026-11-02", "2026-12-01"]:
    d = pd.Timestamp(d); tasks.append(("Retrain and quality gate", "Monthly", d, d + pd.Timedelta(days=3)))
for d in ["2026-10-15", "2026-11-16", "2026-12-15"]:
    d = pd.Timestamp(d); tasks.append(("Rebuild image with patches", "Monthly", d, d + pd.Timedelta(days=1)))
tasks += [("Upgrade libraries and test", "Quarterly", pd.Timestamp("2026-11-09"), pd.Timestamp("2026-11-14")),
          ("Fairness and slice review", "Quarterly", pd.Timestamp("2026-12-07"), pd.Timestamp("2026-12-10")),
          ("Rollback drill", "Quarterly", pd.Timestamp("2026-12-17"), pd.Timestamp("2026-12-18"))]
cal = pd.DataFrame(tasks, columns=["task", "cadence", "start", "end"])
fig = px.timeline(cal, x_start="start", x_end="end", y="task", color="cadence",
                  color_discrete_map={"Weekly": COLORS["teal"], "Monthly": COLORS["indigo"], "Quarterly": COLORS["amber"]})
fig.update_yaxes(autorange="reversed", title=None)
fig.update_layout(height=340, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.15, title=None), xaxis_title=None, margin=dict(l=210))
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

Plan language upgrades early: **Python 3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026**, so any model still pinned to it needs an upgrade path ([Python devguide](https://devguide.python.org/versions/)).

Automate dependency updates with a tool such as Dependabot or Renovate, and let the [MLOps pipeline](/deployment/mlops/mlops-pipelines.qmd) test each update before it merges.

```{.yaml filename=".github/dependabot.yml"}
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: pip
    directory: "/"
    schedule: {interval: monthly}
    groups:
      ml-stack: {patterns: ["scikit-learn", "numpy", "pandas"]}
  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directory: "/"
    schedule: {interval: monthly}
```

## Handling an incident

Some day an alert fires at 2 a.m. A written **runbook** turns panic into a checklist.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TD
  A[Alert fires] --> B{Users affected?}
  B -- no --> C[Open ticket,<br/>fix in working hours]
  B -- yes --> D[Declare incident,<br/>name an owner]
  D --> E{Recent release?}
  E -- yes --> F[Roll back to last<br/>good version]
  E -- no --> G{System or model?}
  G -- system --> H[Scale up, restart,<br/>fail over]
  G -- model --> I[Switch to fallback<br/>rules or older model]
  F --> J[Confirm metrics recover]
  H --> J
  I --> J
  J --> K[Write blameless postmortem]
```

| Severity | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| SEV1 | Payments failing or wrongly declined at scale | Page on-call now, update stakeholders every 30 minutes |
| SEV2 | Quality clearly degraded, users mildly affected | Fix within one business day |
| SEV3 | Early warning, no user impact yet | Ticket, fix this sprint |

: Incident severity levels {#tbl-sev}

The two numbers that matter are **time to detect** (MTTD) and **time to recover** (MTTR). Here is a simulated incident: a bad feature deploy at 14:00 starts declining good customers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-incident
#| fig-cap: "Simulated incident timeline. Good monitoring shortens detection; a ready rollback shortens recovery."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, plotly.graph_objects as go
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
t = pd.date_range("2026-10-01 12:00", "2026-10-01 18:00", freq="min")
m = (t - t[0]).total_seconds() / 60
rate = 1.2 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, len(t))
bad = (m >= 120) & (m < 175)
rate[bad] += 6.5 * (1 - np.exp(-(m[bad] - 120) / 6))
rec = m >= 175
rate[rec] += 6.5 * np.exp(-(m[rec] - 175) / 5)
fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=t, y=rate, line=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], width=2.2), fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(99,102,241,0.12)"))
events = [(120, "bad deploy", COLORS["rose"]), (132, "alert fires", COLORS["amber"]), (160, "rollback starts", COLORS["teal"]), (175, "rollback done", COLORS["teal"])]
for mm, label, c in events:
    fig.add_vline(x=t[int(mm)], line_dash="dot", line_color=c)
    fig.add_annotation(x=t[int(mm)], y=8.6 - 0.75 * events.index((mm, label, c)), text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", xshift=4, font=dict(color=c))
fig.update_layout(height=360, yaxis_title="False-decline rate (%)", showlegend=False, yaxis=dict(range=[0, 9.2]))
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
```

Detection took **12 minutes** and recovery another **43 minutes**. The postmortem should ask how to shrink both: a canary release would have caught the bad deploy on 5% of traffic (see [Updates and versioning](/deployment/update/model-versioning-rollouts.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note}
## A blameless postmortem template
1. **Summary:** what happened, impact, duration.
2. **Timeline:** deploy, detection, decisions, recovery.
3. **Root cause:** the technical cause and why safeguards did not stop it.
4. **What went well:** keep doing it.
5. **Actions:** owner and due date for each fix.
:::

## Write it down: the model card

A short **model card** keeps knowledge alive when people change roles: purpose, training data period, features, metrics by slice, known limits, owner, retraining schedule and runbook link. Store it next to the model in the registry.

## Summary

- Data, concepts, dependencies, infrastructure and knowledge **all decay**.
- Combine **drift-triggered retraining with a maximum model age**.
- Keep a **routine calendar**: weekly reviews, monthly retrains and patches, quarterly upgrades and drills.
- A **runbook, rollback and blameless postmortem** turn incidents into improvements.
- Next: release new versions safely with [Updates and versioning](/deployment/update/model-versioning-rollouts.qmd).
